blocks.content: A CronJob creates a Job automatically, on a recurring schedule, essentially combining everything covered in the Job topic with the familiar scheduling syntax of Unix cron.
1. A Job, Created on a Schedule
blocks.text: 1. A Job, Created on a Schedule

blocks.content: At its core, a CronJob is simple to understand once you know Job, covered in the previous topic, a CronJob is a small wrapper that automatically creates a new Job at each scheduled time, rather than you triggering it manually every time.

blocks.alt: Everything a Job already does, triggered automatically on a schedule

blocks.content:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: nightly-backup
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: backup
              image: backup-tool:1.0
          restartPolicy: OnFailure

code.content:

codes.yaml:

kind: CronJob

  name: nightly-backup

  schedule: "0 2 * * *"

    spec:

        spec:

blocks.content: The schedule field uses exactly the same syntax as traditional Unix cron, 0 2 * * * means "every day at 2am," anyone already familiar with cron already knows how to write a CronJob's schedule.

blocks.alt: The same familiar syntax anyone who has used cron already knows

blocks.content: concurrencyPolicy decides what happens if a scheduled run is triggered while a previous one is still going, Allow (both run simultaneously, the default), Forbid (skip the new run entirely), or Replace (cancel the old run and start the new one).

blocks.alt: Three distinct answers to what happens when a run is still going when the next one is due

blocks.content:
spec:
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid   # never run two backups at once

code.content:
spec:
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid   # never run two backups at once

codes.yaml:
spec:

blocks.content: 4. What Happens if a Run Is Missed
blocks.text: 4. What Happens if a Run Is Missed

blocks.content: If the CronJob controller itself is briefly down and misses a scheduled trigger time, startingDeadlineSeconds decides how late is still acceptable to catch up and run it anyway, versus simply skipping that missed run entirely.

blocks.alt: A deliberate decision about how much lateness is still acceptable to catch up on

blocks.content: A nightly database backup, running automatically at 2am every day without anyone manually triggering it, is exactly the kind of recurring operational task a CronJob is built for.

blocks.alt: A recurring operational task, running reliably without manual intervention

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A CronJob creates a Job automatically on a recurring, cron-syntax schedule, everything Job already provides, triggered without manual intervention.
concurrencyPolicy and startingDeadlineSeconds give real control over overlapping runs and missed schedule windows, worth setting deliberately, not left at their defaults blindly.
